hook: Scripts are fun, but **projects pay**. Four ideas that turn a pile of files into something shippable.

scenes.title: Every **.py file is a module**

steps.at: Every Python file is a module

scenes.narration: Every Python file is a module, and a folder of modules with an init file is a package. Import loads a module once and binds its namespace to a name — it's closer to C sharp's using plus a static class than to a text include. Import the module, then dot into it: import config, then config dot database. You can also import specific names, or star — though star pollutes your namespace and breaks tooling; avoid it in real code.

actors.t: the whole ecosystem expects np / pd

steps.at: import the name when it won

scenes.narration: Three import styles. Import the full path — most explicit. From-import — shorter at call sites, and the style you'll use for packages you own. And aliases: numpy as np, pandas as pd — these aren't optional style; the whole ecosystem expects them. One rule: import the module when names might collide, import the name when it won't.

scenes.title: The **src layout** — learn it once
scenes.sub: Code in src/, tests beside it, config at root

steps.at: A src folder holding your package
this matters because it forces imports
Configuration — pyproject, readmes, dot env — at the root

scenes.narration: Here's the folder layout the ecosystem converged on. A src folder holding your package — this matters because it forces imports to go through the installed package instead of accidently importing from the current folder. Tests in their own tree. Configuration — pyproject, readmes, dot env — at the root. Small projects can skip src, but start with it and you'll never have the 'works from one folder but not another' disease.

steps.at: always imported by its full name

scenes.narration: Picture it top to bottom. The project root holds configuration, readme, environment. Inside, src contains your actual package — always imported by its full name, myproject dot services dot users. Each module owns one domain. And tests mirror the package tree, one test file per module. This shape works for a hundred-line tool and a ten-thousand-line service.

scenes.title: Relative imports: **avoid them**
scenes.sub: Absolute imports always — circular imports bite silently
scenes.narration: Python allows relative imports — dot dot for parent, single dot for sibling. They work, until you move a file or run a script directly, and then they explode. The community rule: absolute imports, always — from myproject dot services import users. The second classic failure is circular imports — module A imports B, B imports A. Python handles some cycles, but the fix is architectural: extract the shared piece into a third module both import.

Memorize the left column as don't, the right as do. And when you see an import error that mentions partially initialized module — that's the circular import. The cure isn't reordering imports; it's moving the shared code — usually models or constants — into its own module that both sides import. Dependencies then flow one direction, always.

scenes.title: if __name__ == "__main__"
scenes.sub: The most-typed line in Python, explained in 30 seconds

steps.at: Every module has a hidden variable, dunder name
When Python runs a file directly
that variable equals the string main
When the file is imported instead
if name equals main wraps code

scenes.narration: Every module has a hidden variable, dunder name. When Python runs a file directly, that variable equals the string main. When the file is imported instead, it equals the module's name. So the idiom if name equals main wraps code that should only run as a script — demos, test data, CLI behavior. It's how one file can be both an importable library and a runnable tool.

steps.at: Python dash m runs a module

scenes.narration: Three ways to run. Python dash m runs a module as main — the reliable way during development. Then the grown-up path: declare a console script in pie project, and after install your command exists on the path. And the development trick of the trade — editable install. Your package behaves as if fully installed, but every edit takes effect immediately. This is your daily workflow from now on.

quiz.why: __name__ is "__main__" only when the file is executed directly; on import it's the module name — so the guard separates script behavior from library behavior.

quiz.q: What's the recommended fix for a circular import (A imports B, B imports A)?
opts: Extract the shared code into a third module both import
quiz.why: Reordering hides the symptom; restructuring removes the cycle — shared models/constants move to a module C that A and B both depend on.

quiz.q: Why does the src layout matter?
opts: It prevents accidental imports from the current working directory
quiz.why: With code under src/, your package must be installed to be imported — no more 'works from one folder, breaks from another'.

code.title: Project skeleton + safe entry point
code.body:
# layout:
# myproject/
#   pyproject.toml
#   src/myproject/__init__.py
#   src/myproject/config.py
#   src/myproject/services/__init__.py
#   src/myproject/services/users.py
#   tests/test_users.py

# --- src/myproject/services/users.py --------------------------
from __future__ import annotations

_users: dict[str, dict] = {}

def add(name: str) -> dict:
    _users[name] = {"name": name}
    return _users[name]

def count() -> int:
    return len(_users)

# --- src/myproject/cli.py --------------------------------------
from myproject.services import users

def main() -> None:
    users.add("ada")
    print(f"{users.count()} users")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()          # runs only when executed directly,
                    # not when imported

# --- pyproject.toml --------------------------------------------
# [project.scripts]
# myproject = "myproject.cli:main"

# dev workflow:
#   uv pip install -e .        # editable install
#   myproject                  # now a real command
annot: Absolute import (myproject.services...) — works from any directory, any entry point
The __main__ guard means tests can import cli.py without side effects
uv pip install -e . = develop mode; changes are live immediately

notes:
# Modules & Project Structure

## Import system
- Every `.py` = a module; folder + `__init__.py` = a package.
- `import a.b` → bind namespace · `from a import b` → bind name · `import x as y`.
- Avoid `from x import *` (pollutes namespace, breaks tooling).
- Standard aliases: `np` (numpy), `pd` (pandas), `plt` (matplotlib).

## Folder layout (src layout)
```
myproject/
  pyproject.toml
  src/myproject/
    __init__.py
    services/users.py
  tests/test_users.py
```
- src layout forces imports through the installed package.

## Relative vs absolute
- ❌ `from . import users` — breaks on moves/direct execution.
- ✅ `from myproject.services import users` — always.
- Circular imports → **extract shared code to a third module**.

## Entry points
- `__name__ == "__main__"` → True only when run directly.
- Run during dev: `python -m myproject.cli`.
- Ship a command: `[project.scripts]` in pyproject.toml.
- Daily driver: `uv pip install -e .` (editable install).
